28 What may be observed with light waves but not with sound waves?
A
diffraction
B
interference
C
polarisation
D
reflection

hints: Notice the question compares light waves with sound waves - recall that light is a transverse wave while sound in air is a longitudinal wave.
Connect this to polarisation, which concerns the plane of oscillation of a transverse wave perpendicular to the direction of travel.
Check diffraction, interference and reflection against the rule that they are shown by all types of progressive wave, transverse and longitudinal.
walkthrough: Identify the wave types: light is a transverse electromagnetic wave with oscillations perpendicular to travel, while sound in air is a longitudinal wave with oscillations parallel to travel.
State the rule for polarisation: polarisation restricts the oscillations to one plane perpendicular to travel, so it can only occur if the wave already has transverse oscillations.
Apply this to sound: a longitudinal wave oscillates only along the direction of travel, so it has no transverse plane to restrict and cannot be polarised.
Check the other three effects: diffraction through gaps, interference of two coherent waves, and reflection at a boundary are general wave behaviours shown by both transverse and longitudinal waves.
Therefore only polarisation is observed with light but not with sound. This is option C.

A.explanation: Diffraction is shown by all waves. Sound waves diffract strongly round doorways and light waves diffract at narrow slits.

B.explanation: Interference is shown by all waves. Two coherent sound sources and two coherent light sources can both produce interference patterns.

C.explanation: Polarisation confines transverse oscillations to one plane. It is possible for transverse light waves but not for longitudinal sound waves.

D.explanation: Reflection is shown by all waves. Both light waves from a mirror and sound waves as an echo can be reflected.
